items.followUp: What are coenzymes? Give one example.

rubric.why: A cofactor is identified as a non-protein substance needed for enzyme activity.
rubric.description: Defines cofactors as non-protein components required for enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition.

rubric.why: A valid example completes the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of a cofactor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: Cofactors are non-protein components required for the activity of certain enzymes.
For example, Mg2+ ions can act as cofactors.

rubric.why: Metabolism refers to the complete set of chemical reactions in an organism.
rubric.description: Defines metabolism as the sum total of chemical or biochemical reactions in an organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the central definition.

rubric.why: Metabolism includes both synthesis and breakdown reactions.
rubric.description: Mentions anabolism and catabolism as the two kinds of metabolic reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both processes.

modelAnswer: Metabolism is the sum total of all the chemical reactions taking place in an organism.
It includes anabolism (building up substances) and catabolism (breaking down substances).

items.followUp: How does the stomach mechanically digest food?

rubric.why: Churning is produced by the muscular activity of the stomach.
rubric.description: States that stomach muscles contract to churn food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the muscular contractions.

rubric.why: Churning mixes food with gastric juice and helps break it into smaller pieces.
rubric.description: Explains the mixing or mechanical breaking action of churning.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its effect.

modelAnswer: Churning is the mechanical mixing and breaking up of food by muscular contractions of the stomach.
It mixes the food with gastric juice.

items.followUp: Where are villi found, and how do they help absorption?

rubric.why: Villi are characteristic projections on the inner lining of the small intestine.
rubric.description: Defines villi and identifies their location.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition and location.

rubric.why: Their main function is to increase absorptive surface and take up digested nutrients.
rubric.description: States the function of villi in absorption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the function.

modelAnswer: Villi are tiny finger-like projections on the inner lining of the small intestine.
They increase the surface area for absorption of digested nutrients into the blood and lymph.

items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps water move from roots to leaves.

rubric.why: Transpiration pull originates from water loss by evaporation from leaves.
rubric.description: Identifies evaporation or water loss from leaves as the cause.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the cause.

rubric.why: The pull draws water upward through xylem from roots toward leaves.
rubric.description: Explains the upward movement of water through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the effect and direction.

modelAnswer: Transpiration pull is the pulling force created when water evaporates from the leaves.
It pulls water upward from the roots to the leaves through the xylem.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and function of the cell membrane.

rubric.why: The membrane forms the boundary around the cell's contents.
rubric.description: States that the cell membrane surrounds the cell or cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its position or role as a boundary.

rubric.why: The membrane is composed mainly of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins.
rubric.description: Describes its basic composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the bilayer or lipid-and-protein composition.

rubric.why: Selective permeability is a defining property of the membrane.
rubric.description: Identifies the membrane as selectively permeable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: The membrane regulates exchange between the cell and its surroundings.
rubric.description: Explains that it controls substances entering and leaving the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its transport-control function.

modelAnswer: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible boundary that surrounds the cytoplasm.
It is mainly made of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it.
The membrane is selectively permeable.
It controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

items.followUp: State the rules for writing the genus and species names in binomial nomenclature.

rubric.why: Binomial nomenclature names each organism with two parts: its genus and species.
rubric.description: Defines binomial nomenclature as a two-part scientific naming system.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the definition, including the two-part nature of the name.

rubric.why: A standard scientific name can be used internationally.
rubric.description: Explains that names are universal or internationally accepted.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this significance.

rubric.why: Standard names avoid confusion caused by different common or local names.
rubric.description: Explains that it prevents confusion from common or local names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this significance.

rubric.why: The two names help identify and classify organisms, including their genus.
rubric.description: States that the name identifies the organism or indicates its genus and species grouping.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this significance.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two-word scientific name: the first word is its genus and the second its species.
It provides a standard name that is used internationally.
It avoids confusion caused by different common or local names.
The two-part name identifies an organism and shows the genus to which it belongs.

items.followUp: Explain oxidation and reduction using an electron-transfer example.

rubric.why: Oxidation is defined as loss of electrons.
rubric.description: Defines oxidation in terms of electron loss.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Reduction is defined as gain of electrons.
rubric.description: Defines reduction in terms of electron gain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Oxidation and reduction occur together in a redox reaction.
rubric.description: States that oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for their simultaneous occurrence.

rubric.why: A valid example demonstrates one substance being oxidized while another is reduced.
rubric.description: Gives an example and correctly identifies the oxidized and reduced substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example with correct identification.

modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, while reduction is the gain of electrons.
Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously in a redox reaction.
For example: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO.
Magnesium loses electrons and is oxidized, while oxygen gains electrons and is reduced.
